Plan · Concept

Progression & stakes

Shithead is luck-heavy, and a run has no rising pressure or real risk yet. This is a structure where luck decides single hands but your decisions decide the run, the way poker tournaments work.

The gap

Why Balatro pulls you forward

Balatro

  • A target that rises: each round demands a bigger score, and you can see it.
  • Your build is the answer: you only meet the number by improving your deck and jokers.
  • Real stakes: fail once and the run is over.
  • Choices soften the luck: shops, rerolls and deck thinning.

Bonehead today

  • Difficulty is a menu, not a climb: tables can be played in any order.
  • The score doesn't matter: it's a number on screen. (The Ferryman's toll is a first taste of stakes.)
  • Tricks are nice to have, not needed to win.
  • One hand is mostly the deal.
The structure

The descent

  1. Climb down through the crypt

    Six floors (the two rooms are a start). Each floor offers two tables to choose from, one safer and one harder that pays more, and ends with a boss. About 12 tables, 30–40 minutes.

  2. Two separate goals

    • Survive: win the hand to move on. Lose and you lose a bone. You start with three; lose them all and the run ends. Lives suit a luck-heavy game better than one strike.
    • Score to buy power: your score converts to gold teeth. Runs, burns, speed and bonus goals pay more, and a lost hand still pays a little.

  3. A shop between floors

    • Buy trick cards from the pool of about 20.
    • Build your deck: remove low cards, or add enchanted cards that only work for you (a gilded 7 adds mult, a glass 10 burns then shatters).
    • Buy ways to manage bad luck: redeal your starting hand, peek at a blind card.
    • Buy a bone back, at a steep price.

  4. Difficulty that actually rises

    Opponents get sharper floor by floor, and later ones cheat with their own tricks. "The house always cheats." Bosses break a rule, reusing the rule-change rounds:

    The MorticianThe pile can't be burned.
    Baron Bones2s don't reset.
    The LichPlays with an open hand but holds five cards.
    The CollectorTakes one of your tricks if you lose.

  5. Reasons to go back after winning

    Grave Depths difficulty levels, each adding a modifier; new starting decks and characters; and the Daily Deal, the same seeded descent for everyone.

How it feels

A moment from a run

Floor 3. Two bones left, 34 gold teeth, a Pyromaniac and Ash Collector build. The harder route pays double, but its boss is the Mortician, who stops burns, and burning is your whole plan. Spend 20 teeth on a Rigged Deck to protect yourself, or save for a glass 10?

Before building it

Prove it's fun, cheaply

  1. Prototype behind a dev switch: three floors, lives, teeth, a basic shop of six items, one boss. No art polish.
  2. Watch five to ten testers: do they hesitate in the shop, talk about their build, start another run straight after dying? Does losing a bone feel tense or unfair?
  3. Tune two dials: how much luck decides a hand (hand size, deck makeup), and how fast opponents get harder.

If testers want another run, build it fully. If a bad deal still feels unfair, add more ways to manage luck before adding content.
